title: The Private Papers of Henry Ryecroft
description: Published in 1903 and Gissing's last completed book: the diary of a retired scholar who has escaped Grub Street into a cottage in Devon, and a meditation on literature, poverty and the consolations of a small income.
plot_or_argument: Ryecroft records the seasons, his reading, his memories of London and the Continent, his reflections on the English character and on the death of his friends; the book ends with his death and the quiet dispersal of his library.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
principal_characters: Henry Ryecroft; G. G., the friend who edits his papers; his housekeeper
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text is the dated entry, continuous in its observation. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order.
historical_context: The 1900s, the Edwardian retreat from the city, the cult of the country cottage, and the professional writer's retirement. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1902 and first published in 1903 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: The Private Papers of Henry Ryecroft was Gissing's most popular book and remains the classic English essay on the pleasures of modest leisure; it is the gentlest of his works and the one that best shows his prose at its most fastidious.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Constable in April 1903; the papers had appeared in The Fortnightly Review and in the American periodicals between 1901 and 1903. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: In the Year of Jubilee
description: Published in 1894 and Gissing's most ambitious study of the new generation of women: the story of Nancy Lord, a Camberwell girl of the Jubilee year whose secret marriage tests the new freedoms of her generation.
plot_or_argument: Nancy Lord, the half-educated daughter of a Camberwell piano dealer, is courted by the vulgar, energetic advertising speculator Luckworth Crewe but falls in love with the idle Lionel Tarrant, whom she marries secretly because her father's will would disinherit her if she married young; deserted while Tarrant is abroad, she bears his child alone, and the novel ends with the two reconciled to an unconventional marriage in which they live apart.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
principal_characters: Nancy Lord; Lionel Tarrant; Luckworth Crewe; Stephen Lord; Horace Lord; Jessica Morgan; Mrs Damerel; Samuel Barmby; Beatrice French; Ada Peachey; Arthur Peachey; Fanny French
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text.
historical_context: The 1887-97 years, the Jubilee, the new suburban London, the bicycle and the shop-girl, and the debate on the 'New Woman'. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel; Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: In the Year of Jubilee is the sharpest English novel about the suburban girl of the 1890s and the most critical of the New Woman's pleasures; it is a key text for the study of gender, consumption and the city.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Lawrence and Bullen in November 1894. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: A Child of the Jago
description: Published in 1896 and the most famous English slum novel of the 1890s: the childhood and death of Dicky Perrott in the Old Jago, a handful of courts in Bethnal Green. It is a prose fiction work of 1896 by Arthur Morrison; it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Dicky Perrott grows up in the Jago, steals, is sent to prison, tries to go straight, and is killed by a gang at the age of seventeen; the novel's exact record of the rents, trades, shops and fights of the district is its argument.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.
principal_characters: Dicky Perrott; Old Perrott; Hannah Perrott; Josh Perrott; Father Sturt; Bill Rann; Aaron Weech; Sally Green; Looey
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is cockney dialect rendered phonetically and with great care.
historical_context: The 1890s, the East End of London, the closing of the Old Nichol slum in 1891-95 (the model for the Jago), and the debate between philanthropy and environmental determinism. The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; industrial and condition-of-england novel.
literary_significance: A Child of the Jago is the central English slum novel of the 1890s and the most influential text in the transition from the Victorian social-problem novel to modern working-class fiction; its controversy over heredity and environment made it a reference point for the sociology of poverty.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1896, as novel (three volumes), by Arthur Morrison. Composed between 1895 and 1896. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Tales of Mean Streets
description: Published in 1894 and Morrison's first book: fifteen sketches and stories of the East End, written in a hard, laconic prose and without a trace of charity or sentiment. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Arthur Morrison; it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.
plot_or_argument: The stories move from the comic ('The Red Cow Group', a pub circle of would-be revolutionaries) to the terrible ('On the Stairs', a mother saving for her dying son's funeral; 'Lizerunt', the destruction of a woman by her husband), and the volume ends with 'To Bow Bridge', a walk taken after a funeral.
narrative_structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
principal_characters: Lizerunt, Billy Chope and Sam Cardew ('Lizerunt'); Mrs Curtis and her dying son ('On the Stairs')
literary_form: Collection of short stories; local-colour sketch
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is cockney dialect rendered phonetically and with great care.
historical_context: The 1890s, the East End, the new journalism and the 'cosmopolitan' short story, and the debate on the authenticity of slum writing. The record dates the work as composed in 1894 and first published in 1894 and it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; social inquiry and the documented survey.
literary_significance: Tales of Mean Streets is the finest English collection of slum stories and a founding text of the modern English short story: Kipling, Conrad and Wells all admired it, and its refusal of pity and moral commentary was a decisive break with Dickensian philanthropy.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1894, as collection of short stories, by Arthur Morrison. Composed in 1894. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Martin Hewitt, Investigator
description: Published in 1894 and the second great English detective series of the 1890s: the cases of Martin Hewitt, a professional investigator who works with Scotland Yard rather than against it. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Arthur Morrison; it is catalogued here under Detective Story and the Tale of Detection; Sensation Novel.
plot_or_argument: Hewitt, a stout, genial former lawyer's clerk with an office off the Strand, chronicled by his journalist neighbour Brett, solves cases of stolen documents, disguised swindlers, a case of mistaken identity and a locked-room problem, and the solutions turn on close observation and institutional knowledge rather than genius.
narrative_structure: A narrative of pursuit and deduction, the evidence gathered in sequence and the reversal held for the close. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
principal_characters: Martin Hewitt; Brett, the narrator, a journalist
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of detection: the pursuit narrative with the investigator's account of the evidence, the exact chronology and the reversal at the close. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is cockney dialect rendered phonetically and with great care.
historical_context: The 1890s, the expansion of the Strand Magazine, the new professional detective and the police detective service. The record dates the work as composed in 1894 and first published in 1894 and it is catalogued under detective story and the tale of detection; sensation novel.
literary_significance: Martin Hewitt is the most important English rival to Sherlock Holmes and the founding figure of the 'professional' detective: Morrison's series established the model of the investigator as a working professional that the twentieth-century detective story would develop.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1894, as collection of detective stories (strand magazine), by Arthur Morrison. Composed in 1894. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Hole in the Wall
description: Published in 1902 and Morrison's best late novel: a crime novel of the Wapping riverside, told by the boy who comes to live at his grandfather's tavern, the Hole in the Wall. It is a prose fiction work of 1902 by Arthur Morrison; it is catalogued here under Detective Story and the Tale of Detection; Sensation Novel.
plot_or_argument: Young Stephen Kemp, sent after his mother's death to live with his grandfather Captain Nat, landlord of the Hole in the Wall at Wapping, watches the riverside underworld close around the tavern: Marr, the shipowner whose fraud drowned Stephen's father, absconds with the firm's money and is waylaid by the bully Dan Ogle in a thieves' den; the pocket-book of notes falls into Captain Nat's hands; and Ogle, Musky Mag, the blind fiddler Blind George and Marr's betrayed partner Viney all scheme to recover it, while the old man turns a new bitterness on the men who ruined his son.
narrative_structure: A narrative of pursuit and deduction, the evidence gathered in sequence and the reversal held for the close. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
principal_characters: Stephen Kemp (the narrator); Captain Nat Kemp, his grandfather; Marr; Viney; Dan Ogle; Musky Mag; Blind George
literary_form: Novel; detective story, first issued in 1902
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of detection: the pursuit narrative with the investigator's account of the evidence, the exact chronology and the reversal at the close. The author's characteristic manner is cockney dialect rendered phonetically and with great care.
historical_context: The 1900s, the Port of London and its river trades, the London docks and their casual labour, and the child witness in the English courts. The record dates the work as composed between 1901 and 1902 and first published in 1902 and it is catalogued under detective story and the tale of detection; sensation novel.
literary_significance: The Hole in the Wall is one of the finest English novels of the Thames and the docks, and a key example of the child's-eye detective narrative that would be developed by Dickens's and Stevenson's successors.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1902, as novel, by Arthur Morrison. Composed between 1901 and 1902. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Illustrations of Political Economy
description: Published monthly from February 1832 to 1834 and Martineau's first great success: twenty-five fictional case studies designed to teach the principles of political economy to ordinary readers through stories of wages, prices, population and the poor law.
plot_or_argument: Each tale takes a single economic principle and shows its working in the life of a family or a village: 'The Hill and the Valley' on capital and labour, 'A Manchester Strike' on combinations, 'Weal and Woe in Garveloch' on population, 'Cousin Marshall' on the poor laws.
narrative_structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close.
principal_characters: Ella of Garveloch ('Ella of Garveloch'; 'Weal and Woe in Garveloch'); William Allen ('A Manchester Strike')
literary_form: Series of twenty-five tales in monthly parts
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is the exemplary narrative with a documented argument.
historical_context: The 1830s, the Reform Act and the new political economy of Malthus and Ricardo, the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834, and the mechanics' institute movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1832 and 1834 and first published in 1832 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel, it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: The Illustrations made political economy a popular literature: they sold tens of thousands of copies, were translated across Europe, and invented the fictional case study as a form of public education — the direct ancestor of the social-problem novel and of the documentary tradition.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1832, as series of twenty-five tales in monthly parts, by Harriet Martineau. Composed between 1832 and 1834. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Society in America
description: Published in 1837 after a two-year tour and the most systematic English account of the United States before Tocqueville's English readership: a study of American politics, religion, education, class, family life and slavery.
plot_or_argument: Martineau examines the machinery of American democracy — the constitution, parties, the press, the churches, colleges, commerce — and tests it against the condition of women, the treatment of the black population and the state of the poor, concluding that the country has failed its own principles in each case.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the exemplary narrative with a documented argument.
historical_context: The 1830s, Jacksonian democracy, the abolitionist movement and the mob violence of 1835, and the 'woman question' in America. The record dates the work as composed between 1834 and 1836 and first published in 1837 and it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: Society in America founded the comparative sociology of the United States and is the most important English book about American society between Birkbeck and Bryce; its chapters on the 'non-existence' of women and on slavery were used by the American feminist and abolitionist movements.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1837, as sociological study in three volumes, by Harriet Martineau. Composed between 1834 and 1836. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Deerbrook
description: Published in 1839 and Martineau's finest novel: the life of two sisters in a provincial town, and a study of middle-class English society, courtship and professional ambition. It is a prose fiction work of 1839 by Harriet Martineau; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
plot_or_argument: Hester and Margaret Ibbotson come to live at Deerbrook with their aunt; Hester marries the surgeon Edward Hope, Margaret is loved by the misanthropic Mr Grey, and the novel follows the small society of the town through gossip, jealousy, illness and the death of the doctor.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
principal_characters: Hester Ibbotson; Margaret Ibbotson; Edward Hope; Mr Grey; Mrs Enderby; Philip Enderby; Maria Young; Morris the surgeon
literary_form: Novel (three volumes); realist novel of common life
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the exemplary narrative with a documented argument.
historical_context: The 1830s, the provincial town and its dissenting chapel, the medical profession, and the position of unmarried women. The record dates the work as composed between 1838 and 1839 and first published in 1839 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; novel of development and the growth story.
literary_significance: Deerbrook is the most accomplished English provincial novel before Middlemarch and one of the first novels to treat the social life of a town as a subject in its own right; its picture of the gossip and mutual surveillance of village society is a landmark of English realism.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1839, as novel (three volumes), by Harriet Martineau. Composed between 1838 and 1839. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Hour and the Man: A Historical Romance
alternative_titles: Hour and the Man: A Historical Romance
description: Published in 1841 and the first English novel to take a black revolutionary as its hero: a fictional life of Toussaint Louverture and the Haitian revolution. It is a prose fiction work of 1841 by Harriet Martineau; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Toussaint, the former slave who becomes the leader of the revolution in Saint-Domingue, is shown in council, in battle and in his household, and the novel follows the uprising, the French expedition of 1802 and Toussaint's betrayal and death in the prison of Fort de Joux.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
principal_characters: Toussaint L'Ouverture; Margot, his wife; Placide and Isaac, his sons; Génifrède, his daughter; Moyse, his nephew; Henri Christophe; Jean-Jacques Dessalines; General Leclerc
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the exemplary narrative with a documented argument.
historical_context: The 1790s, the Haitian revolution, the abolitionist movement of the 1830s-40s, and the British emancipation of 1833. The record dates the work as composed between 1840 and 1841 and first published in 1841 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; social inquiry and the documented survey.
literary_significance: The Hour and the Man is the founding English novel of the Haitian revolution and the first substantial fictional treatment of a black leader in English literature; it was read by abolitionists on both sides of the Atlantic and marks the limit of what a British novelist in 1841 could say about slave revolution.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1841, as historical novel (three volumes), by Harriet Martineau. Composed between 1840 and 1841. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Life in the Sick-Room: Essays
description: Published in 1844 and written out of Martineau's own long illness: a series of essays on the experience of invalidism, which she treats as a condition with its own duties, liberties and spiritual possibilities.
plot_or_argument: The essays address the sick person's relation to visitors, to doctors, to religion and to the world outside the sickroom; they attack the 'theology of consolation' that treats illness as a punishment and argue for the invalid's authority over her own life.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the exemplary narrative with a documented argument.
historical_context: The 1840s, the Victorian sickroom, the doctrine of resignation, and Martineau's own case (a uterine tumour and, later, deafness and heart disease). The record dates the work as composed between 1843 and 1844 and first published in 1844 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
literary_significance: Life in the Sick-Room is the founding English text of the literature of illness: it invented the first-person essay on being ill as a subject, and its arguments against the consolations offered to invalids were taken up by later feminist and disability writing.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1844, as collection of essays, by Harriet Martineau. Composed between 1843 and 1844. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Autobiography of Harriet Martineau
description: Written from the 1850s and published after her death in 1877, with a memorial by Maria Weston Chapman: one of the greatest Victorian autobiographies, and a completely unsentimental account of a working literary life.
plot_or_argument: Martineau recounts her Unitarian upbringing, the loss of her fortune, her deafness, her career, her American journey, her religious doubts, her mesmeric illness and her old age, and gives exact and often devastating verdicts on the public figures she knew.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
principal_characters: Harriet Martineau, the narrator; James Martineau, her brother; Henry George Atkinson; Charlotte Brontë; Wordsworth; Carlyle
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is the exemplary narrative with a documented argument.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Victorian life-writing tradition, and the posthumous publication arranged by her friend Maria Weston Chapman. The record dates the work as composed between 1855 and 1876 and first published in 1877 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
literary_significance: Martineau's Autobiography is the classic Victorian record of a woman's professional self-making and a model of unsentimental self-analysis; its judgments on her contemporaries make it a primary source for the literary history of the period.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1877, as autobiography (published posthumously in three volumes), by Harriet Martineau. Composed between 1855 and 1876. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: 'Criminals, Idiots, Women and Minors': Is the Classification Sound?
description: Published in Fraser's Magazine in December 1868 and the most effective single piece of Victorian feminist polemic: an argument against the legal classification of married women with criminals, idiots and minors.
plot_or_argument: Cobbe takes the legal doctrine of coverture and reads it literally: the married woman can make no contract, hold no property, sue no one and be sued by no one, exactly like the lunatic and the infant; she demonstrates the consequences through cases of deserted and abused wives and demands the reform of the law.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the documented essay with statistics and case evidence.
historical_context: The 1868 debate on the Married Women's Property Bill, the doctrine of coverture, and the case of the deserted wife. The record dates the work as composed in 1868 and first published in 1868 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: 'Criminals, Idiots, Women and Minors' is one of the founding documents of English feminism and gave the campaign for the Married Women's Property Acts its most memorable argument; the essay is still the standard short statement of the legal position of the Victorian wife.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1868, as periodical essay (fraser's magazine, december 1868), by Frances Power Cobbe. Composed in 1868. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: 'Wife-Torture in England'
description: Published in the Contemporary Review in 1878 and the most important Victorian essay on domestic violence: a documented account of wife-beating in England, with cases from the police courts and the assizes.
plot_or_argument: Cobbe collects the evidence of the courts over several years, shows that wife-beating is treated as a trivial offence, argues that the law's reluctance reflects the doctrine of the wife's submission, and proposes the flogging of convicted wife-beaters — a proposal she defends against the objections of her own allies.
narrative_structure: A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is the documented essay with statistics and case evidence.
historical_context: The 1870s, the campaign that produced the Matrimonial Causes Act amendment of 1878, the police courts, and the debate over corporal punishment. The record dates the work as composed in 1878 and first published in 1878 and it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: 'Wife-Torture in England' created the public vocabulary for domestic violence and was directly responsible for the 1878 legislation that allowed magistrates to separate battered wives from their husbands; it is the founding text of the English literature on domestic abuse.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1878, as periodical essay (contemporary review, april 1878), by Frances Power Cobbe. Composed in 1878. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Hopes of the Human Race, Hereafter and Here
alternative_titles: Hopes of the Human Race, Hereafter and Here
description: Published in 1874 and Cobbe's most systematic work of religious speculation: an argument for a moral universe that survives the collapse of orthodox Christian doctrine. It is a prose work of 1874 by Frances Power Cobbe; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.
plot_or_argument: Cobbe examines the evidence for immortality, the problem of evil, the future of the human race and the moral argument for a progressive afterlife, and defends a theism grounded in conscience rather than revelation or miracle.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the documented essay with statistics and case evidence.
